questions.q: A jet's cruise constraint moves to a higher altitude at the same Mach number. Its bucket on the T_SL/W_TO vs W_TO/S diagram moves:
questions.a: Up by 1/α and toward lower W_TO/S, since q falls
w: Down, since the air is thinner and drag falls
Right, since true airspeed rises at altitude
Up only, with the bucket wing loading fixed
questions.x: At fixed Mach q = ½γpM² falls with altitude, so the bucket W/S = (q/β)√(C_D0/K) moves left, while the falling thrust lapse α lifts the whole curve.

questions.q: With a parabolic polar, the minimum T_SL/W_TO on the level cruise constraint curve equals:
questions.x: The bucket value is (β/α)·2√(KC_D0), and 2√(KC_D0) is exactly 1/(L/D)_max, so level flight at best L/D needs thrust equal to weight over (L/D)_max.

questions.q: A twin must meet a climb gradient with one engine inoperative. Plotted as total installed T_SL/W_TO, the thrust loading the live engine must supply is:
questions.x: The remaining engine supplies all the thrust, so the installed total is N/(N − 1) times the live engine requirement, which is 2 for a twin.

questions.q: For a propeller aircraft, the constraint diagram vertical axis is usually:
questions.x: A propeller engine is rated by shaft power, so each constraint is written as P_SL/W_TO = (T/W)V/η_p versus W_TO/S.

questions.q: Cruise constraint: q = 12,000 Pa, β = 0.9, C_D0 = 0.02, K = 0.05. At what W_TO/S does the curve reach its minimum (bucket), in Pa?
questions.x: The bucket sits where parasite and induced terms are equal, βW_TO/S = q√(C_D0/K), so W_TO/S = (12,000/0.9)·√0.4 ≈ 8433 Pa.

questions.q: Complete the stall constraint, a maximum wing loading
questions.x: Stall lift balances the current weight βW_TO, so ½ρV_stall²C_Lmax = βW_TO/S gives the wing loading limit.

questions.q: Match each master equation term to the requirement that makes it nonzero or large
pairs: Gear, flaps, stores or drag chute
questions.x: A turn raises n in the induced term, climb adds the potential energy rate, acceleration adds the kinetic energy rate, and C_DR carries extra drag items.

questions.q: Put the master equation derivation steps in order
steps: Write the power balance (T − D − R)V = W d/dt(h + V²/(2g))
Expand D/W with the polar, using C_L = nW/(qS)
Substitute T = αT_SL and W = βW_TO and solve for T_SL/W_TO
questions.x: The energy balance divided by WV gives thrust over weight, the polar fills in drag, and α and β refer everything to sea-level thrust and takeoff weight.

questions.q: A jet climbs to a higher altitude at the same weight. Its minimum thrust required and the speed where it occurs:
questions.a: Same D_min = W/(L/D)_max, at a speed higher by √(ρ₀/ρ)
w: D_min falls, at the same speed
D_min rises by ρ₀/ρ, at the same speed
D_min falls by √(ρ/ρ₀), at a lower speed
questions.x: Minimum drag occurs at the fixed C_L for (L/D)_max, so its value W/(L/D)_max stays put while the speed holding that C_L scales as 1/√ρ.

questions.q: At the same weight, minimum power required at altitude compared with sea level:
questions.x: At fixed C_L, drag is unchanged and speed scales as 1/√ρ, so P = DV grows by √(ρ₀/ρ).

questions.q: For a jet with thrust independent of speed, the steepest climb angle occurs at:
questions.x: sin γ = (T − D)/W, and with T flat the excess thrust peaks where D is smallest, at (L/D)_max.

questions.q: In a steady unpowered glide, the minimum sink rate occurs at:
w: Maximum C_L, at the stall speed
questions.x: Sink rate equals power required over weight, DV/W, so it is smallest at the minimum power condition, the same point as propeller maximum endurance.

questions.q: Battery electric aircraft range, R = (e*/g)η(L/D)(m_battery/m), differs from the Breguet fuel range because:
questions.a: Mass stays constant, so range is linear in battery mass fraction
w: Mass falls, so range has a logarithm
Range grows with flight speed V
questions.x: A battery keeps its mass as it discharges, so the weight integral collapses to a straight product, and the best range is flown at (L/D)_max.

questions.q: W/S = 4000 Pa, ρ = 0.9 kg/m³, C_D0 = 0.02, K = 0.05. Find the minimum drag speed V_md in m/s (1 decimal).
Complete the maximum lift to drag ratio for C_D = C_D0 + KC_L²
questions.x: At C_L = √(C_D0/K) the two drag terms are equal, C_D = 2C_D0, giving (L/D)_max = 1/(2√(KC_D0)).

questions.q: At fixed C_L and altitude, match each quantity to how it scales with weight W
pairs: Takeoff ground roll at fixed S and T
questions.x: Holding C_L fixes L/D, so D ∝ W, V ∝ √(W/S), power ∝ W^(3/2), and ground roll ∝ V²/(T/W) gives W².

questions.q: The same aircraft flies heavier with the same limit load factor. On its EAS V-n diagram the corner speed V_A:
questions.x: V_A = √(2n_limit W/(ρ₀SC_Lmax)), so more weight needs more dynamic pressure to reach the limit load on the stall curve.

questions.q: At 10 km, ρ/ρ₀ = 0.34. In true airspeed, the corner speed there compared with sea level is:
questions.x: The corner speed is fixed in EAS, and V = V_e/√(ρ/ρ₀) = V_e/√0.34 ≈ 1.71V_e.

questions.q: FAR 25 sets the negative limit maneuvering load factor at:
questions.x: Transports must reach n = −1.0 up to V_C, tapering linearly to zero at V_D.

questions.q: Where on the V-n diagram is the aircraft aerodynamically limited?
questions.a: Along the stall curves, at speeds below V_A
w: Along the limit load lines, between V_A and V_D
Along the gust lines above V_C
questions.x: Below the corner speed the wing reaches C_Lmax before the limit load, so lift capacity, set by aerodynamics, bounds the envelope.

questions.q: Sustained level turn: q = 9000 Pa, W/S = 3000 Pa, T/W = 0.40, C_D0 = 0.02, K = 0.1. Find the sustained load factor n (3 decimals).
Complete the gust alleviation factor in terms of the airplane mass ratio μ_g
questions.x: K_g = 0.88μ_g/(5.3 + μ_g) scales the sharp-edged gust down for the aircraft's finite response time; it rises toward 0.88 for heavy, highly loaded wings.

questions.q: Match each certification category to its positive limit load factor
questions.x: FAR 23 sets 3.8, 4.4 and 6.0 for normal, utility and aerobatic; FAR 25 uses 2.1 + 24000/(W + 10000) bounded between 2.5 and 3.8, so heavy transports sit at 2.5.

questions.q: Put the V-n diagram design speeds of a typical transport in increasing order
questions.x: V_A = V_S1√n_limit, about 1.6V_S1 for n_limit = 2.5, cruise follows, and the dive speed closes the envelope on the right.

questions.q: The thermal efficiency of an ideal turbojet depends only on:
questions.a: The total compression temperature ratio τ_rτ_c
questions.x: η_th = 1 − 1/(τ_rτ_c): heat is added and rejected along isobars between the same pressure levels, so the overall pressure ratio sets the efficiency.

questions.q: Ideal turbojet at fixed compressor pressure ratio: raising T_t4 makes specific thrust and TSFC:
questions.x: More heat per unit air raises the jet velocity and specific thrust, while η_th stays fixed and η_p falls with the faster jet, so TSFC rises.

questions.q: Ideal turbojet at fixed T_t4: specific thrust versus compressor pressure ratio:
questions.a: Peaks at an intermediate value, where τ_c = √τ_λ/τ_r
questions.x: Low π_c gives poor thermal efficiency and high π_c leaves little room for heat addition below T_t4, so the work peaks at τ_rτ_c = √τ_λ.

questions.q: The compressor and turbine span similar pressure ratios. Why does the Brayton cycle still deliver net work?
questions.a: Isobars diverge on T-s, so the hot turbine drop exceeds the compressor rise
w: The turbine has a higher isentropic efficiency
The nozzle adds work to the shaft
questions.x: Along an isobar dT/ds = T/c_p, so the isobars spread apart at high temperature and the same pressure ratio spans a larger ΔT at the turbine.

questions.q: An engine flies at V₀ = 250 m/s with overall efficiency η_o = 0.35 on fuel with h_PR = 43 MJ/kg. Find TSFC in mg/(N·s), 2 decimals.
questions.x: η_o = FV₀/(ṁ_f h_PR) gives TSFC = V₀/(η_o h_PR) = 250/(0.35·43×10⁶) = 1.661×10⁻⁵ kg/(N·s).

questions.q: Complete the isobar slope on a T-s diagram, from T ds = dh − v dp
questions.x: At constant pressure T ds = c_p dT, so isobars climb with slope T/c_p and spread apart as T rises.

questions.q: Match each engine performance measure to its definition
pairs: Rate of jet kinetic energy gain over fuel heat rate
Thrust power FV₀ over rate of jet kinetic energy gain
Thrust power FV₀ over fuel heat rate
questions.x: The overall efficiency is the product η_th·η_p, and TSFC = V₀/(η_o h_PR) ties fuel burn to it.

questions.q: Order these engines from highest to lowest specific thrust F/ṁ at the same T_t4
questions.x: Specific thrust tracks the jet velocity increment, which is largest with reheat and smallest when the energy is spread over a large bypass mass flow.

questions.q: The Kutta condition states that:
questions.a: Flow leaves a sharp trailing edge smoothly, fixing the circulation
w: Circulation is constant around any closed curve
Downwash is uniform over an elliptic wing
questions.x: Among the infinitely many potential flows around an airfoil, the one with smooth flow off the trailing edge selects a single Γ, and with it the lift.

questions.q: For an elliptic spanwise lift distribution, the induced angle of attack along the span is:
questions.x: Elliptic loading gives constant downwash w = Γ₀/(2b), so every section sees the same α_i = C_L/(πAR).

questions.q: In thin airfoil theory, the aerodynamic center of a cambered airfoil lies at:
questions.x: Thin airfoil theory gives c_m,c/4 independent of α for any camber, so the quarter chord is the aerodynamic center.

questions.q: Adding aft sweep to a wing at fixed AR tends to:
questions.a: Raise M_crit, lower lift slope, and promote tip stall
w: Lower M_crit and raise lift slope
Move the stall inboard and raise C_Lmax
questions.x: Only the normal Mach component M cos Λ drives compressibility, while spanwise flow thickens the outboard boundary layer and loads the tips.

questions.q: In linearized supersonic theory, a thin flat plate has lift slope:
questions.x: Ackeret theory gives c_l = 4α/√(M∞² − 1), which falls as Mach rises.

questions.q: Sears-Haack body: A_max = 4 m², length l = 40 m. Find the wave drag area D/q = 9πA_max²/(2l²) in m² (4 decimals).
questions.x: D/q = 9π·16/(2·1600) = 0.1414 m²; wave drag falls as 1/l², so a longer, slimmer body pays far less.

questions.q: Complete the Prandtl-Glauert correction for subsonic lift coefficient
questions.x: Linearized compressible flow stretches the incompressible solution, multiplying pressure coefficients and c_l by 1/√(1 − M∞²).

questions.q: Match each part of the lifting line vortex system to its role
pairs: Carries Γ(y) and produces lift, L' = ρVΓ
Induce downwash and hence induced drag
Left behind with circulation equal and opposite to the bound vortex
One bound segment plus two trailing legs
questions.x: Helmholtz's theorems keep each filament's strength constant, so the bound vortex continues as trailing legs and closes through the starting vortex.

questions.q: In ideal hover momentum theory, the far-wake velocity and area relative to the disk are:
questions.x: Energy gives a far-wake speed of 2v_i, and continuity then halves the slipstream area.

questions.q: Compared with a helicopter, a tiltrotor's much higher disk loading T/A in hover means:
questions.a: Higher induced velocity and more power per unit thrust
w: Lower induced velocity and better power loading
The same hover power at equal weight
questions.x: v_i = √((T/A)/(2ρ)) and T/P = 1/v_i, so small rotors sized for cruise pay in hover power.

questions.q: In forward flight at advance ratio μ, the reverse flow region on the retreating side is:
questions.a: A circle of diameter μR touching the hub
w: An annulus at the blade tips
A circle of radius μR centered on the hub
A sector on the advancing side
questions.x: Local blade speed Ωr + V sin ψ is negative where r < −μR sin ψ, which traces a circle of diameter μR on the retreating side.

questions.q: Vortex ring state is entered in:
questions.a: Powered vertical descent at a rate near the hover induced velocity
w: Fast forward flight at high advance ratio
questions.x: Descending into its own downwash, the rotor recirculates its wake into a toroidal vortex, giving thrust fluctuations and high power.

questions.q: A rotor gives T = 10,000 N at sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³) with disk area A = 50 m² and absorbs 140 kW. Find the figure of merit (3 decimals).
Complete the ideal hover power loading
questions.x: P_ideal = Tv_i, so thrust per unit power equals 1/v_i, and lower disk loading gives more thrust per watt.

questions.q: Match each unusual vehicle to the driver that sizes it
pairs: Very thin air: large fast rotors capped by tip Mach
Dense air and low gravity make hover cheap
Daily energy balance, with batteries for the night
Approach speed, catapult and arresting loads
questions.x: Each environment changes which constraint binds: density for rotors, energy closure for solar, and deck operations for carrier aircraft.

questions.q: Order these VTOL vehicles from lowest to highest disk loading
questions.x: Hover power per unit thrust grows as √(T/A), so the power starved human powered helicopter uses huge rotors and jet lift uses tiny, fast jets.

questions.q: Why does a forward swept wing have a low divergence speed?
questions.a: Upward bending twists the streamwise tip nose up, adding lift and more bending
w: Its aerodynamic center sits aft of the elastic axis
Its tips stall first at low speed
Its skins are thinner than an aft swept wing
questions.x: Bending torsion coupling gives wash-in on a forward swept wing, a self-reinforcing loop that composite aeroelastic tailoring can counter.

questions.q: A standard flutter remedy is:
questions.a: Mass balance that moves the section CG forward toward the elastic axis
w: Moving the section CG aft of the elastic axis
questions.x: With the CG at or ahead of the elastic axis, inertial coupling between bending and torsion weakens and the flutter speed rises.

questions.q: Transport aircraft keep roll control at high speed, above outboard aileron reversal, by using:
questions.x: Inboard the wing is torsionally stiff, and spoilers reduce lift directly, so both keep their sense where outboard ailerons twist the wing.

questions.q: In the sizing loop, as required range grows, W_0:
questions.a: Rises faster than linearly, diverging as W_e/W_0 + W_f/W_0 approaches 1
w: Rises with the square root of range
questions.x: The fuel fraction grows exponentially with range through Breguet, and W_0 = W_payload/(1 − W_e/W_0 − W_f/W_0) amplifies it.

questions.q: Typical section: moving the aerodynamic center closer to the elastic axis (smaller e) makes the divergence dynamic pressure:
w: Stay the same, since q_D depends on K_θ alone
questions.x: A shorter moment arm e means lift produces less twist for the same torsional stiffness, so divergence moves to a higher q.

questions.q: Typical section: K_θ = 50,000 N·m/rad, e = 0.1 m, a = 5 /rad, S = 4 m². Find the sea level divergence speed (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³) in m/s, 1 decimal.
Complete the takeoff gross weight equation
questions.x: Takeoff weight splits into crew and payload, fuel and empty weight, so fixed weights over the leftover fraction gives W_0.

questions.q: Match each aeroelastic problem to a design remedy
pairs: Raise torsional stiffness or bring the AC toward the elastic axis
Mass balance the section CG forward
questions.x: Each remedy cuts the coupling that drives the instability: stiffness and arm for divergence, control location for reversal, inertia for flutter, ply layup for forward sweep.

questions.q: In wings-level flight in still air, the pitch attitude θ, angle of attack α and flight path angle γ are related by:
questions.x: Rotating up from the horizon by γ reaches the velocity vector, and a further α reaches the body axis, so θ = α + γ.

questions.q: In a level coordinated turn at load factor n and speed V, the turn radius is:
questions.x: The horizontal lift component W√(n² − 1) supplies the centripetal force mV²/R.

questions.q: On an energy maneuverability chart, the minimum time to climb path passes through:
questions.a: Points where h_e lines are tangent to P_s contours
w: Points of maximum Mach on each altitude
Points of minimum drag at each altitude
questions.x: Each energy level is gained fastest where P_s = dh_e/dt is largest, which is the tangency point on that h_e line.

questions.q: The point mass equations of motion are written in wind axes because:
questions.a: Lift and drag are defined relative to the velocity vector
w: Gravity acts along the velocity vector
Thrust always aligns with the wind
questions.x: With x along V, drag appears along the path and lift normal to it, so the tangential and normal equations stay simple.

questions.q: Zoom climb with T = D: an aircraft at 250 m/s pulls up and slows to 100 m/s (g = 9.81 m/s²). Altitude gained in m (nearest 1)?
questions.x: Energy height is conserved, so Δh = (V₁² − V₂²)/(2g) = 52,500/19.62 ≈ 2676 m.

questions.q: Complete the horizontal kinematic equation (heading ψ, flight path angle γ)
questions.x: The horizontal speed V cos γ projects onto the x axis by the heading, so dx/dt = V cos γ cos ψ and dy/dt = V cos γ sin ψ.

questions.q: Match each flight angle to its definition
pairs: From the velocity vector to the body x axis
From the horizon to the velocity vector
From the horizon to the body x axis
Bank, rotation about the velocity vector
questions.x: α and γ together make up θ in the vertical plane, and φ tilts the lift vector out of that plane.

questions.q: Put the steps reducing the point mass EOM to a steady climb in order
steps: Write the wind axis point mass equations along and normal to V
Set φ = 0, dV/dt = 0 and dγ/dt = 0, and take α + ε small
Read off T = D + W sin γ and L = W cos γ
Multiply by V/W to get the climb rate V sin γ = (T − D)V/W
questions.x: The steady wings-level assumptions remove the rates and align thrust with the path, and the along-path balance times V/W gives the climb rate as specific excess power.

questions.q: A natural laminar flow airfoil gets low profile drag by:
questions.a: A long favorable pressure gradient that delays transition
w: A sharp leading edge that trips turbulence
A thicker section that raises supervelocity
Suction slots near the trailing edge
questions.x: Accelerating flow keeps the boundary layer stable, holding the lower laminar skin friction over more of the chord.

questions.q: For drag buildup, a wing's wetted area is about:
questions.a: Twice the exposed planform area, slightly more for thicker sections
questions.x: Both upper and lower surfaces are wetted, with curvature adding a little: S_wet ≈ S_exposed(1.977 + 0.52t/c).

questions.q: A typical Oswald efficiency for a conventional subsonic aircraft is:
questions.x: Real span loading, fuselage interference and the lift dependent part of viscous drag pull e below the elliptic value of 1.

questions.q: The hump in a seaplane takeoff is:
questions.a: The peak in water drag just before the hull rises onto the step to plane
w: The airspeed where the floats leave the water
The peak in induced drag near liftoff
questions.x: At low speed the hull displaces water and drag climbs steeply, then once planing begins the wetted area shrinks and drag falls.

questions.q: Scaling a design up at the same speed raises Reynolds number. Its turbulent skin friction coefficient:
questions.x: C_f falls gently as Re rises, so large aircraft enjoy somewhat lower skin friction coefficients and C_D0.

questions.q: Double slotted flap: Δc_lmax = 1.6c'/c with c'/c = 1.25, S_flapped/S_ref = 0.6, hinge line sweep 20°. ΔC_Lmax = 0.9Δc_lmax(S_flapped/S_ref)cos Λ_HL (3 decimals)?
Complete the flat plate transition Reynolds number
questions.x: Transition near Re_x ≈ 5 × 10⁵ means full scale wings, at Re in the millions, are mostly turbulent.

questions.q: Order these trailing edge devices by increasing airfoil Δc_lmax
questions.x: Each slot re-energizes the boundary layer on the next element, so typical increments climb from 0.9 to 1.3, 1.6 and 1.9 times c'/c.

questions.q: The stick-free neutral point lies, relative to the stick-fixed neutral point:
questions.a: Forward, giving a smaller static margin
w: Aft, giving a larger static margin
questions.x: A free elevator floats with the local flow and weakens the tail's restoring lift, which moves the neutral point forward.

questions.q: A stable canard configuration is designed so that:
questions.a: The canard stalls first, dropping the nose before the wing stalls
questions.x: The canard runs at a higher lift coefficient, so it reaches C_Lmax first and the nose drops while the wing still has margin.

questions.q: On an aft tail aircraft, trim drag grows as the CG moves forward because:
questions.a: The tail download rises, so the wing lifts more and induced drag grows
w: The tail lift rises, unloading the wing
questions.x: A forward CG needs more nose-up moment, so the tail pushes down harder and the wing carries weight plus that download.

questions.q: The forward CG limit is usually set by:
questions.a: Elevator power to rotate at takeoff or flare at C_Lmax in landing
questions.x: With flaps down and ground effect the nose-down moment is largest, so the elevator must still trim to C_Lmax with the CG forward.

questions.q: Aft wing sweep contributes to the dihedral effect C_lβ:
questions.a: A negative (stabilizing) value that grows with C_L
questions.x: In sideslip the windward wing sees less effective sweep and more lift, rolling the aircraft away from the slip in proportion to C_L.

questions.q: C_m0 = 0.05, C_mα = −0.8 /rad, C_mδe = −1.2 /rad (δe positive trailing edge down). Elevator angle to trim at α = 0.1 rad, in degrees (2 decimals)?
questions.x: C_m0 + C_mα α + C_mδe δe = 0 gives δe = −(0.05 − 0.08)/(−1.2) = −0.025 rad ≈ −1.43°, a trailing edge up deflection that holds the higher α.

questions.q: Complete the stick-fixed neutral point for a wing plus aft tail
questions.x: Downwash from the wing reduces the tail's angle of attack change by the factor (1 − dε/dα), so the tail contributes less stability.

questions.q: Order these points along the fuselage from forward to aft (typical stable design)
questions.x: Elevator power fixes the forward limit, the aft limit keeps a margin ahead of the stick-free neutral point, and the stick-fixed neutral point lies furthest aft.
